content.p: For about half a century Francesco Mallardo, known to police and neighbours as "Ciccio 'e Carlantonio", stood among the leading figures of the Camorra in the countryside and suburbs north of Naples. He was born in Giugliano in Campania and died on 29 May 2025, aged 74, in a clinic in Parma. Stylo24 counted 33 years served in prison and two spectacular escapes.

He led the Mallardo clan of Giugliano and, according to investigators, was one of three men who founded the Secondigliano Alliance, a federation of Camorra clans that l'Unita says dominated the area north of Naples for years. His life tracks the Camorra's own change, from smuggling and feuds over territory to a holding-style business that, in Stylo24's words, laundered money and invested in property and trade.
content.h2: A murdered father and a feud
content.p: The family's nickname came from the father. Domenico Mallardo was called "Mimi' 'e Carlantonio", and in those years it was normal to add a parent's name to one's own. He was killed in 1967. Fanpage reports that those responsible were never established in court despite several trials, although some informers said the Maisto clan, then dominant in Giugliano, was behind the ambush, with the boss Alfredo Maisto and his three sons taking part. L'Unita says Francesco came from a family of farmers, ran cigarette smuggling for a short time and for years was among the main opponents of Raffaele Cutolo's Nuova Camorra Organizzata.

The feud with the Maisto clan then turned the Mallardo family into the masters of Giugliano. Fanpage lists the Maisto men who died violently: Luigi, Antonio and Enrico. For the killing of Luigi Maisto, a first-instance court sentenced Francesco and his brother Giuseppe Mallardo to 16 years each, along with two Giuliano brothers, described as turncoat bosses of Forcella, who got 9 years and 4 months each. Fanpage adds that, according to a source it names only as "Lovigino", Luigi was killed to help the Mallardo brothers rise and because they also wanted revenge for their father. On appeal, Francesco and Giuseppe Mallardo were acquitted of the crime, Fanpage reports. Stylo24 says the Maisto clan were wiped out and that the Mallardo family then took on a mafia identity, joining the Nuova Famiglia coalition formed against Cutolo.

Investigators say the Alliance was founded in the late 1980s by Eduardo Contini, Francesco Mallardo and Gennaro Licciardi, known as "'a Scigna" (the monkey). Stylo24 dates its birth to the 1990s and names Mallardo, Contini and Patrizio Bosti as the founders. Both outlets agree that marriage held the structure together. Mallardo, Contini and Bosti married three sisters of the Aieta family, which Sky TG24 reported in 2019 when the sisters themselves were described by Naples prosecutors as holding leading roles. Il Mattino, writing in 2003, called him the most charismatic figure of the Alliance, a troika with Contini and Maria Licciardi, the sister and heir of Gennaro.

In June 2019 more than 100 precautionary measures were carried out against alleged members of the Contini, Mallardo and Licciardi clans, with about 130 million euros of assets seized. Charges included mafia association, money laundering, drug trafficking, extortion and smuggling. The prosecutor of Naples, Giovanni Melillo, said the women of the Alliance kept contact with bosses held under the strict 41 bis prison regime and took important decisions themselves. Those arrested were suspects at that stage; the 2019 reporting does not give verdicts.

On the night of 23 March 1992, police in Giugliano found Mallardo, then a fugitive, in an anonymous attic flat on the seventh floor of a block on the edge of town. Antonio De Iesu, then head of the local police station and later Naples police chief, told Fanpage and ilSud24 that Mallardo lived modestly, with no luxury cars, and had told neighbours he ran a cleaning business. They learned who he was only when summoned to the station. He did not resist. De Iesu recalled asking him whether it would not have been better to live on bread and onions, and being told: "Dotto', è 'o destino" (translation ours: it is fate). A few hours later carabinieri stopped a car at a checkpoint nearby and caught Licciardi, who, De Iesu said, had been sheltering in a flat close to Mallardo's.

Mallardo was later sent to the high-security prison in Parma, where he suffered a heart attack. According to Gazzetta del Sud, that illness won him house arrest in May 1999, and on 8 September 1999 he escaped from the hospital in Giugliano. Stylo24 adds a second escape, from a clinic in Pinerolo, and says he was listed among the 30 most dangerous fugitives in Italy.

In April 2000 police raided a farmhouse in Giugliano where, according to Gazzetta del Sud, in its report of 15 April, a summit of the Alliance was under way over a meal of broad beans, pancetta and sausage. Thirteen men sat at the table. Mallardo pretended to have a heart attack. Arrested with him were Feliciano Mallardo and Patrizio Bosti of the Contini group, and the owner of the house, Carlo Granata, who had no criminal record. Gazzetta del Sud called Feliciano Mallardo his brother; later reports, including l'Unita, call him his cousin, a point the sources leave unresolved.

The same paper noted that Mallardo had been sentenced to seven years for mafia association and was on trial in several cases, among them the kidnapping of the son of the Grimaldi shipowners. The head of government, Massimo D'Alema, called the raid good news. The raid came shortly after the seizure of ten property and trading companies worth about 100 billion lire, in which, the paper wrote, the clan's proceeds were invested, drug trafficking first among them.

His last capture came at the end of August 2003. Il Mattino reported that police stopped a car at kilometre 12,500 of the Naples-Bari motorway, coming back from a holiday with his wife, daughters and two grandchildren. Mallardo pretended to stop, then accelerated to about 180 kilometres an hour with his family inside, until another patrol made him slow down and a single pistol shot hit a tyre. The paper described him as one of five of the most dangerous bosses, on the Viminale's list of 30 most wanted fugitives. Of the troika, Il Mattino noted, only Contini was still free.

Prison did not end the clan's work, according to investigators. A 2015 ANSA report on a crackdown by 400 financial police described alleged control over a bakery business and investments in car sales, construction and financial services along the Licola, Varcaturo and Lago Patria coast, with companies worth eight million euros seized. Among those charged was a public-health psychiatrist, accused of issuing false medical certificates for another jailed boss, Vincenzo D'Alterio. Stylo24 reports that investigators wrote in 2015 that he kept running the clan by exploiting his illnesses. In the same piece it says 74 bank accounts worth 12 million euros were confiscated nine years before his death.

The Mallardo business reached beyond Giugliano. In May 2011 the Guardia di Finanza arrested Feliciano Mallardo, nicknamed "o sfregiato" (the scarred one) and described by il Giornale as the clan's current regent, in an operation in Lazio and Campania that seized assets, taken from affiliates of the Mallardo and Casalesi clans, estimated at 600 million euros, including about 300 flats in Rome to a coffee-roasting plant at Castel Volturno. Il Fatto Quotidiano wrote that the clan's seized property in the previous year topped one billion euros, and recorded a turncoat's claim, not proved, that the clan steered Giugliano's council.

That claim returned in February 2025, when the Carabinieri's ROS arrested 25 people, 20 of them jailed and five placed under house arrest, including a former mayor, Antonio Poziello. They were accused, to varying degrees, of mafia association, political-mafia electoral exchange over the September 2020 municipal election, extortion, usury and corruption. ANSA reported that the clan's income supported members, including those in prison, and their families. These were accusations at the time of reporting.

Stylo24 says Mallardo had spent nine years under 41 bis and had been granted semi-liberty days before he died. Fanpage gives a different version. Serving 30 years, he left prison a few days before his death for a rehabilitation clinic in Emilia-Romagna, where he was held under house arrest. The request had been filed three months earlier; the house arrest was granted on 27 May. He was terminally ill and on palliative care. His lawyer, Gian Paolo Schettino, confirmed the death to Fanpage.

Stylo24 instead puts his death in the clinical ward of Parma prison, where it says he was being treated for a terminal tumour. The accounts do not agree on where he was held when he died. His brother Giuseppe was still in prison, and Feliciano had died in 2015, according to Fanpage.
